data.source_title: Nurse Staffing and Inpatient Hospital Mortality
data.locator: Methods, Data and Population and Patient Turnover definition; Results, Characteristics of Patients, Units, and Staffing; Table 1
data.source_setting: 43 units at a tertiary academic medical center in the United States; adult general-care, step-down, and intensive-care units were included, with specified unit exclusions.
data.source_n: 197,961 admissions; 176,696 staffed unit-shifts, of 3,227,457 total patient-unit-shift records.
data.quantity: Observed patient turnover per staffed unit-shift; high-turnover classification frequency

value.high_turnover_rule: unit shift turnover rate >= that unit day-shift mean + 1 SD

data.unit: percent of shift census for turnover rate; SD in percentage points; high-turnover count and percent of staffed shifts
data.source_evidence_basis: Observed shift-level admissions, transfers, discharges, census, and staffing from hospital electronic systems. The article defines turnover as admissions + transfers + discharges (deaths excluded) divided by adjusted/start-of-shift census, so complete turnover equals 100%. High turnover is a shift rate >= the unit-specific day-shift mean + 1 SD; Table 1 reports 12,242 (6.9%) of 176,696 staffed shifts.
data.limitations: Single high-quality academic center with relatively high average staffing and lower-than-predicted mortality; historical 2003–2006. The high-turnover threshold is relative to each unit day-shift mean, not a portable absolute rate. Do not import 6.9% as a local threshold or benchmark without local calibration.
data.inferred_scenario_use: For sensitivity analysis only, a simulation may define high-turnover shifts using the paper’s relative rule (unit day-shift mean plus one SD) and compare the study’s observed 6.9% frequency; do not make this the target-hospital rule or infer patient outcome effects locally.
